title: Masei: cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–15)
hook: six cities where one who killed by accident could flee

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah paused its list of journeys to give one exact date of death, Aaron's, on the first of Av. Your line was dates are remembered. Whose date did you mark? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

A second of distraction on a wet road. A ladder that wasn't tied down. An accident that ends a life, and nobody meant it. In the ancient world, that wasn't the end of the story. A relative of the person who died might come looking for blood, and many societies expected him to. The Torah doesn't pretend that anger away. But as the people stand at the edge of the land, it sets aside something no one had asked for: six cities, built for the person who did the worst thing they never meant to do.
screen: `AN ACCIDENT, AND NOBODY MEANT IT.` → `A RELATIVE COMES LOOKING.` → `SIX CITIES SET ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the law, in paraphrase. When you cross the Jordan, choose cities to be cities of refuge, so that someone who kills a person by accident can flee there. Six in all: three east of the Jordan, three in the land of Canaan. And they're open to everyone: to Israelites, and to the stranger and the settler living among them. The Hebrew is ir miklat, a city of refuge, of shelter. The person who fled there was safe from the avenger, and would have a proper trial. If the death was found to be an accident, they lived in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, and then they could go home. The rabbis took this law and made it humane in surprising detail. The Talmud says the roads to the cities had to be kept in good repair, and at every crossroads a sign was posted reading refuge, refuge, so that a frightened person running for their life would never take a wrong turn. The cities had to have water and markets, and be neither too small nor too crowded. If a student had to flee there, the Talmud says, his teacher went with him, so he wouldn't be cut off from learning. And the mothers of the high priests, it says, brought food and clothing to the people in the cities, so they wouldn't pray for the high priest to die. None of this pretends the death didn't happen. The person still lived away from home for years. But a mistake didn't have to end in another death. There was a road, signposted, to somewhere safe.
screen: `IR MIKLAT: A CITY OF REFUGE.` · `SIX CITIES, OPEN TO THE STRANGER.` · `REFUGE, REFUGE, AT EVERY CROSSROADS.` · `A TEACHER GOES WITH HIS STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make room for someone's mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who did something that hurt you, or hurt others, without meaning to. A careless word, a dropped responsibility, an honest mistake with real consequences. Notice the part of you that wants them to pay. Let it be there. Then ask: is there a road to refuge I could leave open for them? Not pretending it didn't happen, but not chasing them either. Picture a small sign at the crossroads. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masei. The portion that sets aside six cities of refuge, open to Israelite and stranger alike, for those who killed by accident.
Your line: a place of refuge. Today, when someone admits a mistake to you, make your first words ones that leave them somewhere safe to stand. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: The cities of refuge are read in the portion of Masei in midsummer, and their laws are studied in the Talmud tractate Makkot, which describes the roads, signs and care for those who fled there.

original.note: Hebrew: a city of refuge, of shelter (Numbers 35:11).

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient hiding place for criminals.
what it means: cities where someone who killed by accident could live safely and be judged fairly.
what a scholar hears: Makkot 10a–b says the roads were kept wide and signposted 'miklat, miklat', a teacher was exiled with his student; Makkot 11a tells of the high priests' mothers bringing food.

notes: Makkot 10a (cities need water and markets, neither too large nor too small; teacher exiled with student), 10b (roads repaired, 'miklat miklat' signs at crossroads), 11a (high priests' mothers provided food and clothing); confirm.
Return home at the death of the high priest: Numbers 35:25, 28.
'Open to the stranger and the settler': Numbers 35:15 (ger and toshav).
